name: OnceHub
tagline: Publish booking pages with routing rules, forms, and reminders

tiers.name: Basic
tiers.limits: 1 user; 1 calendar; 1 booking link; 6 weeks of analytics/activity history.

tiers.name: Schedule
tiers.limits: Unlimited booking links, calendars, and meetings; 1 phone number.

tiers.name: Route
tiers.limits: Unlimited routing forms and responses; 2 phone numbers.

tiers.name: Engage
tiers.limits: Unlimited chatbots and conversations; 3 phone numbers.

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: Designed for 30+ users; Security & Compliance add-on included.

pricing.freeTierCaps: 1 user; 1 calendar; 1 booking link; 6 weeks of analytics/activity history.
pricing.hiddenCosts: Security & Compliance costs $6/user/month monthly or $5/user/month annually outside Enterprise; extra phone numbers cost $4/month; SMS uses separately purchased credits.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For OnceHub, publish booking pages with routing rules, forms, and reminders. The hard boundary is routing depth, calendar integrations, crm workflows, and dependable scheduling, plus calendar integrations and reliability.
coreLoopDIY: Read one calendar, publish booking pages with availability, routing rules, and forms, create conflict-safe bookings, and send confirmations and reminders.
whatYouLose: routing depth, calendar integrations, CRM workflows, and dependable scheduling
ongoingBurden: OAuth refresh, webhooks, timezone databases, race conditions, reminders, deliverability, privacy, and uptime
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for OnceHub because people pay because one double booking or missed invite can cost more than years of subscription fees. The recurring cost buys OAuth refresh, webhooks, timezone databases, race conditions, reminders, deliverability, privacy, and uptime, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Cal.com
priorArt.desc: Mature open-source scheduling platform with calendar integrations and booking workflows.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Cal.com Free
rejectedAlternatives.desc: The free tier covers one person; routing forms and team assignment are paid.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Cal.diy
rejectedAlternatives.desc: The open-source fork removed the very Teams and Workflows features this comparison needs.

rejectedAlternatives.name: YouCanBookMe Free
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Forms and confirmations survive on free, but routing rules do not.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Schedule plan and a single-user booking service DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for OnceHub in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, Google Calendar OAuth, and Resend; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: read one calendar, publish booking pages with availability, routing rules, and forms, create conflict-safe bookings, and send confirmations and reminders.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Implement one account with configurable working hours, buffers, minimum notice, and booking horizon.
Connect Google Calendar using OAuth and store refresh tokens encrypted at rest.
Calculate availability in UTC and render it in the visitor's detected timezone.
Reserve slots transactionally, create calendar events, and prevent concurrent double booking.
Send confirmation, cancellation, and reminder email with signed management links.
Add an admin booking list, event-type editor, audit log, and calendar reconnect flow.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out Microsoft and Apple calendar support.
Deliberately leave out team round-robin routing.
Deliberately leave out payments, CRM workflows, and enterprise controls.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
